**8.5.3** The finished and adding new item are attached under that folder. The first file is ex-generated by the designer as a blank window in Figure 8.54, and the second file is auto-generated by the Relational Designer and it contains code to create a child class **CSE_DEPTDataContext** that is derived from the DataContext class. Four overloaded constructors of the child class **CSE_DEPTDataContext** are declared in the class.

To Open the Relational Designer, double-click on the item **CSE_DEPT.dbml** from the Server Explorer window. The opened Relational Designer is shown in Figure 8.54.

Prior to creating the entity class, we need to connect to our sample database. To do that, just click the arrow in front of our database, **dept-24jpuph/sql/2019.express.cse_DEPT.dbo**, and then expand the **Tables** folder to see all five tables.

To create an entity class for each table, perform a drag-place operation for each table between the Server Explorer window and the blank Designer. Starting from the **Login** table, drag it from the Server Explorer window and place it into the Design view. By dragging the **Login** table designer, the entity class is created and added into the **CSE_DEPT.designer.cs** file. You can then use this entity class to create and manipulate data from the project to the Login table in our sample database **CSE_DEPT**.

Perform similar drag-place operations to all other tables, and the finished designer is shown in Figure 8.55. The arrow between tables is an association that is a new terminology used in the LINQ to SQL, which represents the relationship between tables.

Now we can use these entity classes and the DataContext to perform desired data actions against our sample database using the LINQ to SQL technique.

Let's start from our **Login** page to access the **Login** table in our sample database.

## 8.7.2 PERFORM LINQ TO SQL QUERY TO LOGIN TABLE VIA LOGIN PAGE

First we need to create a field variable **cse_dept** based on our Derived Context class **CSE_DEPTDataContext**. As discussed, this object is used to connect to our sample database. For overloaded constructors are available for this DataContext class, but in this application we use only the simplest one to simplify our coding process.

**Figure 8.56** The codes for the creation of the field variable.

Our new project **WebLINQSQL Project** and the code window of the **Login.aspx** page, and enter the codes shown in Figure 8.56 into this code to see how it works.

Let's have a closer look at this piece of codes to see how it works.

- A. The namespace **System.Linq** is automatically added into this code section and we need to use all data related to LINQ to SQL and this namespaces all of them.
- B. A new instance of our derived class **CSE_DEPTDataContext** is created with the first constructor. This entity class is generated under our current project, this namespace **WebLINQSQL_Project** must be prefixed for that class. Otherwise a compiling error would be encountered.

A trick here is that no connection string is included in this connection object. Yes, where is the connection string? How can we connect to our database without connection string? While, the connection string is in there. Where? Ok, let's have a closer look at it this issue now.

Open our web configuration **Web.config** which is located at the Solution Explorer by double-clicking on it. A sample file is shown in Figure 8.57.

It can be found from this XML file that our connection string is in there under the `<ConnectionString>` tag, which includes the Data Source and the database Provider. In this application, it is a full name for our Data Source, including the database server, database name and authentication mode. Here a **Windows Authentication Mode** is used.

When you create new instance of our derived **DataContext** class to connect to our database, the system can automatically load this connection string from this configuration file and it to connect even when we did not clearly indicate this string. The instance **cse_dept** has finished the database connection when we created it and this has been saved during the creation process. Now we can use this connection object to perform our data actions against our sample database.

Double-click on the **Login** button from the Design View of the **Login** page to open its Click event method, and enter the codes shown in Figure 8.58 into this method.

```csharp
private void cmdLogin_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
{
    string username = string.Empty;
    string password = string.Empty;
    Selection selfform = new Selection();
    var loginfo = (from log in cse_dept.Tables where log.username == txtUsername.Text && log.password == txtPassword.Text select log).FirstOrDefault();
    if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(txtUsername.Text) || string.IsNullOrEmpty(txtPassword.Text))
    {
        Response.Write("<script>alert('Enter username and password!');</script>");
    }
    else if (loginfo != null)
    {
        Response.Redirect("Selection.aspx");
        cse_dept.Close();
        cse_dept.Dispose();
    }
    else
    {
        Response.Write("<script>alert('Login failed!');</script>");
    }
}
```

- C. A trick here is that no connection string is included in this connection object. Yes, where is the connection string? How can we connect to our database without connection string? While, the connection string is in there. Where? Ok, let's have a closer look at it this issue now.
